name: GitHub style: a 43-second network partition moves the primary to the West Coast (2018-10-21)
description: Web and API path: users → DNS → GLB Director (L4) → HAProxy (L7) → Rails app → authorization service, Memcached, MySQL. Writes also go into a webhook queue, and workers send them to external receivers. The MySQL primary and two replicas are on the East Coast, two more replicas on the West Coast; replication is asynchronous. orchestrator promotes a replica when the primary is unreachable. On 2018-10-21 at 22:52 UTC, maintenance to replace optical equipment cut the East Coast data center off from the network hub for 43 seconds. orchestrator promoted a West Coast replica. The East Coast primary had a few seconds of writes not yet replicated to the West Coast (954 in one busy cluster), so it could not fail back safely. After the network came back, every write from the East Coast apps crossed the country; pages were slow and the service was degraded for 24 hours 11 minutes. Sources: https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/oct21-post-incident-analysis/ , https://github.blog/engineering/infrastructure/glb-director-open-source-load-balancer/ , https://github.blog/engineering/infrastructure/mitigating-replication-lag-and-reducing-read-load-with-freno/ , https://github.blog/engineering/infrastructure/stretching-spokes/ . Parameters are small values for teaching.

notes.text: Try this: 1) Run the scenario: at 30 s the East Coast is cut off and every request fails from 30 to 73 s (the app is on the East Coast too). At 50 s orchestrator promotes a West Coast replica; 932 writes not yet replicated there are lost (real incident: 954). At 73 s the network is back, but the primary stays on the West Coast: every write crosses the country and back, the Rails app goes from 67% to 90% busy, and p99 goes from about 120 ms to about 165 ms. 2) Set the MySQL failover time to 60 s (longer than the partition): no failover, no lost writes, and everything is normal after 73 s. Users see the same outage, because the app is in the region that was cut off. 3) Set it back to 20 s and lower the replication delay from 3000 ms to 300 ms: about 110 writes are lost. 4) Give the Rails app 8 instances: it absorbs the cross-country latency, but the writes are still lost.

Simplified: the real incident was a network partition; the East Coast primary was still alive and took writes for a few seconds. Here it is a region outage. The old primary comes back as a replica at once; comparing the data and restoring from backups (24 hours in the real incident) is not simulated. There is no semi-synchronous replication and no rule to fail over only within a region. Webhooks were paused during the incident and over 5 million piled up; here there is only the queue and the workers.
